newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Saudi Arabia unlikely to swap oil for U.S. fighters.
newsitem.headline: Saudi Arabia unlikely to swap oil for U.S. fighters.

text.p: Saudi Arabia, the world's leading arms importer, is unlikely to swap its oil to pay for a new generation of U.S. fighters, industry experts said on Wednesday.
Saudi Arabia was not discussing an oil-for-arms trade and Riyadh and Washington were not close to completing a deal which has been under discussion for eight years, experts said.

Western media reports have said Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil producer and exporter, would seek to emulate its 1980s al-Yamamah oil-for-arms deal with Britain but one expert said the kingdom had "learnt its lesson and this is the end of it".
The multi-billion dollar al-Yamamah contract involves Saudi Arabia swapping some 400,000 barrels of its daily oil output for Tornado fighters from British Aerospace.
There has been speculation that Lockheed Martin Corp would land a similar contract to supply 100 F-16 long-range fighters worth up to $10 billion for oil supplies of a similar value.

"Why should Saudi Arabia go back to a middleman who gets a commission? Like this, Aramco will have full control over when, where and for how much to sell the oil," one expert familiar with the negotiations said.

State-owned Saudi Aramco, the world's largest oil company, "will sell the oil, proceeds go to a trust fund at SAMA (Saudi Arabian Monetary Agency or central bank) and then SAMA pays for the aircraft," the expert said.

From January 1, as part of its strategy of gaining greater control of its exports and generating higher income, Aramco assumed responsibility for selling some 400,000 bpd which had been marketed internally by British oil majors Shell and BP under the original terms of the Al-Yamamah deal.
Officials at Lockheed Martin International in Riyadh, contacted by Reuters, declined to say anything about the deal.

Riyadh's main interest, like that of the Gulf emirate of Abu Dhabi, is in a fully-loaded F-16 although it has also looked at a newer version of the F/A-18 strike aircraft made by McDonnell Douglas Corp bought by Kuwait, experts said.
Bahrain is the only Gulf Arab state to operate F-16s.

"Even if (Defence and Aviation Minister) Prince Sultan gives the go ahead it will take a long time, maybe more than a year, before all the approvals are finalised and both sides work out the details," one expert said.
Saudi Arabia, the emerging military power on the Arab side of the Gulf shared with Iran, started taking delivery of 72 F-15S, a downgraded model of the McDonnell Douglas F-15E, in late 1995.
Delivery of the F-15S, worth some $9 billion, is expected to be completed in less than three years.
Saudi Arabia concluded arms transfer accords worth $57.2 billion in the 1988-95 period compared to $75.9 billion in 1987-94.
